item.title: AI may not work like the human brain after all, scientists discover
item.description:
# AI may not work like the human brain after all, scientists discover Date:November 21, 2026Source:York UniversitySummary:AI may not think like the human brain after all, according to a striking new discovery that challenges how scientists understand artificial intelligence.
"Artificial intelligence systems are often described as 'brain-like' because they can predict activity in parts of the brain that help us recognize objects," says York University Assistant Professor Kohitij Kar, senior author of a new study.
Kar warns that this distinction could become increasingly important as artificial intelligence advances.
Artificial intelligence is increasingly used to help researchers design experiments, study human behavior, and investigate neurological and psychological conditions.
Similar artificial intelligence models are already being used to study hearing, language, and movement.
Published in _Nature Machine Intelligence_, the study introduces a new approach to evaluating artificial intelligence that goes beyond measuring how well a system performs a task.

## Missouri S&T plans to launch the 120-credit-hour program in the fall of 2027, pending state approval, preparing students for careers in the growing artificial intelligence industry. The University of Missouri Board of Curators on Thursday unanimously approved a new bachelor's degree program in artificial intelligence at Missouri University of Science and Technology in Rolla, paving the way for what will be the first standalone undergraduate AI degree offered in Missouri.
Students will learn from a curriculum that combines computer science, mathematics, data science and ethics with specialized artificial intelligence coursework.
"Our graduates will be prepared to understand and innovate within modern engineered systems that are increasingly using AI."
Students will study programming, algorithms, machine learning, data science, computer organization, databases and cybersecurity.

item.title: If AI Does the Junior Work, How Will Young People Become Experienced?
item.description:
# If AI Does the Junior Work, How Will Young People Become Experienced? ## Poluhina: Artificial intelligence is replacing the work that beginners do, limiting opportunities for graduates to develop judgment and experience. ![](https://www.the74million.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/ai-taking-entry-level-jobs.jpg) The 74/Getty Images
By [Nadia Poluhina](https://www.the74million.org/contributor/1042552/)November 22, 2026
The views expressed here are those of the author.
- [![](https://cdn.flipboard.com/badges/flipboard_mbsw.png)](https://share.flipboard.com/bookmarklet/popout?v=2&title=If%20AI%20Does%20the%20Junior%20Work%2C%20How%20Will%20Young%20People%20Become%20Experienced%3F%20%E2%80%93%20The%2074&url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.the74million.org%2Farticle%2Fif-ai-does-the-junior-work-how-will-young-people-become-experienced%2F&t=1795348805269&utm_campaign=tools&utm_medium=article-share&utm_source=www.the74million.org)
_Get stories like this delivered straight to your inbox._ [**Sign up for The 74 Newsletter**](https://www.the74million.org/about/newsletters/?utm_source=website&utm_medium=article&utm_campaign=top&utm_id=newsletter)
Those are very different parts of my life, but lately they have led me to the same question: How do people develop judgment and experience if [artificial intelligence](https://www.the74million.org/tag/artificial-intelligence/) starts doing more of the work through which beginners used to gain them?
Early in my career, I built financial models, checked numbers and prepared presentations. More experienced colleagues reviewed what I’d done, sometimes sending me back to reconsider an assumption that looked perfectly reasonable on paper. With enough practice and feedback, I learned that a correct calculation can still lead to a poor decision.
That work was producing two things at once: an output and a more experienced person. The company received something useful, and I gradually became capable of handling more complicated problems.
AI may change the economics of that arrangement.
Junior employees contribute useful work while they learn, helping offset the cost of supervising them. If AI can produce an initial analysis more cheaply, a company may decide it no longer needs as many beginners. The savings are immediate, while developing experienced staff takes years. And even after investing in someone, the employer cannot be certain that person will stay.
A company could automate junior assignments now and hire experienced professionals when it needs them. That may be a reasonable decision for one business. But if enough companies make the same choice, where will those experienced workers come from?
There are early signs that entry-level hiring is changing. A U.S. These include such jobs as junior software engineers, financial analysts, graphic designers and marketing associates. Neither study proves that AI caused these changes or measures employers’ investments in training.
AI may also help beginners learn faster, and some companies may find better ways to train people with it. We cannot assume, however, that every employer will continue to find it worthwhile to hire inexperienced workers.

So anytime an AI software gets built or AI technology gets built, the first thing that happens to train that AI is you need people to create the data that it learns from. So people have to teach every AI, whether that’s, you know, Reddit or Facebook information or newspaper information, teaching a large language models to folks using CAPTCHA, if you’ve ever used CAPTCH and said, you know, put a box around, tell me where all the traffic lights are. And those people with AI, especially for government technology or for critical AI technology that is for critical usage, you’re important, you need high reliability and high accuracy. And so we don’t hallucinate or the AIs work functionally.
